page: Amazon Web Services m1.medium is a legacy first-generation general-purpose cloud instance built on the Xen hypervisor and utilizing the 32-bit i386 processor architecture. The instance provides 1 dedicated physical core and 1 vCPU powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 CPU running at a base clock frequency of 1.8 GHz. Memory allocation is set at 4.0 GB, accompanied by 410 GB of bundled local HDD storage. The instance includes no GPU acceleration and reports a baseline network bandwidth of 0 Gbps.

Across synthetic compute and memory benchmarks, the m1.medium demonstrates performance constrained to the lower percentiles. The single vCPU yields a stress-ng score of 1284.79 and Geekbench scores of 489.0 for single-core and 491.0 for multi-core evaluation, placing it in the bottom 10 percent of tested instances. Memory throughput reaches 7.84 GB/s for large uncached reads and 6.77 GB/s for uncached writes. Application-level benchmarks show 0.45 million Redis SET operations per second and 1.13 GB/s in static web serving throughput.

From a cost-efficiency and architectural standpoint, the instance offers legacy support but low computational density relative to modern standards. The CPU lacks modern instruction sets such as AVX and AVX-512, while the bundled storage relies on rotational magnetic media rather than solid-state drives. These hardware specifications make the instance suited primarily for running legacy 32-bit software systems, basic batch utilities, and low-traffic environments requiring local scratch disk capacity without high IOPS demands.
